text: A surplus is what is left over once you have taken all you need — more of something than you can use. The word turns up far beyond food: a country can run a surplus of money, a team a surplus of players. Here one farm near Leipzig ended the season with 4,000 tonnes of potatoes beyond anything it could sell.

Optimal does not just mean good — it means the best possible for one particular purpose. Weather that is optimal for potatoes would ruin a beach day, and that is the point: optimal always depends on what you are trying to do. Germany got rain and temperatures landing exactly where potato plants like them.

To oblige someone is to make them do something, because a rule, a law or a duty leaves them no real choice. It sits between asking and forcing: nobody drags you, but saying no is not on offer. Frederick’s decree obliged Prussian farmers to give up part of their fields to potatoes whether they liked the crop or not.

Kartoffel is the German word for potato and Flut means flood, so Kartoffel-Flut is a nickname Germans made up for this year: the potato flood. German often glues two words together into one long word like this. Nothing is actually flooding — it is a joke about potatoes arriving in such huge amounts.

A spud is simply a potato. It is an informal word, the kind you would hear in a kitchen or a market rather than in a science book. Writers use it, as this one does, to avoid saying potato in every single sentence.

Taters is another casual word for potatoes, made by chopping the front off potato. English does this a lot — telephone becomes phone, hamburger becomes burger. The restaurant had a whole tonne of taters to hand out.

A tuber is the fat underground part of a plant where it stores food for itself, and a potato is exactly that. It is not a root and not a seed: it is a swollen stem packed with starch, which is why it is so filling. Farmers growing more tubers means more land planted with crops like potatoes.

Cultivation means growing plants on purpose — preparing soil, planting, watering and harvesting — rather than finding them growing wild. A plant under cultivation is one people look after. The article uses it twice: more potato cultivation in Germany now, and the first potato cultivation the Spanish found in South America.

On the road a yield sign tells you to give way, but in farming a yield is how much a field actually produces — the amount harvested from a given patch of land. A yield 17% higher than usual means the same fields handed over noticeably more potatoes than they normally do. The two meanings share an old idea: giving something up or handing something over.
Owing to means because of. It has nothing to do with owing money, even though it looks like it. Writers use it to point at the cause of something: the harvest was huge owing to the weather.

You may know bounty as reward money for catching someone, but its older meaning is a generous amount of something, especially food from the land. A good harvest is a bounty. Belgium, France and the Netherlands had one too, meaning they also got far more than usual.

A tonne is a metric unit of weight: 1,000 kilograms, which is about 2,200 pounds — roughly a small car. So 22 tonnes of potatoes is about the weight of a school bus, and 4,000 tonnes is an amount no farm could eat or store. Britain and most of the world spell it tonne to separate it from the slightly lighter American ton.

To dish something out is to hand it round to lots of people, the way food gets spooned onto plates. It works for things other than food too — a teacher can dish out homework, a referee can dish out penalties. The restaurant had a tonne of potatoes to dish out to anyone who wanted them.

The Berliner Tafel is Berlin’s best-known food bank, a charity that has collected spare food and passed it to people who need it since 1993. Tafel is the German word for table, and Berliner just means of Berlin. Taking 22 tonnes of potatoes in one go is the sort of thing only an organisation with vans and cold storage can do.

A food bank is a charity that gathers food that would otherwise be thrown away — spare harvests, unsold bread, donated tins — and gets it to people who cannot afford enough to eat. It is the middle piece between food nobody will sell and families who need it. Without one, a farm with thousands of spare tonnes would have to find hungry people on its own.

An abundance of something is a large, comfortable amount of it — plenty, with more to spare. It is a warmer word than surplus, which points at the leftovers; abundance points at the plenty itself. The writer’s joke is that if you had to be buried in one crop, the potato is the one to pick.

A calorie is a unit measuring the energy your body gets from food. Calorie-dense means a food packs a lot of that energy into a small weight, so it fills you up fast. A potato is calorie-dense next to lettuce: you would have to eat a whole bag of leaves to match one baked potato.

If something lends itself to a use, it suits that use well and works easily for it. Nothing is being lent or borrowed — the phrase just means it fits. A potato lends itself to an enormous number of meals: mash, chips, soup, dumplings, pancakes.

Relative to means compared with. A relative can be a cousin or an aunt, but in this phrase relative keeps its other sense: measured against something else. Saying the potato is calorie-dense relative to other vegetables means it holds more energy than they do, not that it is stuffed with energy on some absolute scale.

Conquistadors were Spanish soldiers and explorers who sailed to the Americas in the 1500s and seized huge stretches of land for Spain, often violently. The word is Spanish for conquerors. They are in this story because they were the first Europeans to see potatoes being farmed, and ships carried the crop back across the Atlantic.

The Andes are the long mountain range running down the western edge of South America, through countries such as Peru, Bolivia and Chile. People there were growing potatoes thousands of years before Europeans arrived. High mountain fields are cold and thin-soiled, and the potato is one of the few crops that thrives in them.

A staple food is the plain, everyday food a whole region eats most of and gets most of its energy from — rice in much of Asia, bread and potatoes in much of Europe, maize in parts of Africa. Staples are cheap, filling and store well. Saying the potato became a staple worldwide means it stopped being a curiosity and turned into a daily meal for millions.

Small potatoes is an old expression for something unimportant or not worth much fuss. So saying a thing is no small potatoes means it matters a great deal. The writer is having fun here: the potato’s part in human history is genuinely large, and the potato pun is deliberate.

A blight is a disease that spreads through plants and kills them, and a blighted crop is one wrecked by it. In Ireland in 1845 a mould-like organism spread field to field and rotted the potatoes in the ground. People also use blighted for hopes or plans ruined by something.

To emigrate is to leave your own country to live somewhere else for good. The matching word from the other side is immigrate, which means arriving in a new country — same journey, different end you are standing at. Almost three million people emigrated from Ireland after the potatoes failed, which is why so many families in America trace a line back there.

A famine is not one hungry day but food running short across a whole region for long enough that people starve and die. Famines usually follow a ruined harvest, a war, or people being too poor to buy what food remains. Frederick the Great pushed potatoes on his farmers precisely to keep one from happening.

A decree is an order given by a ruler that carries the force of law the moment it is announced — no parliament, no vote, no discussion. Kings and emperors ruled largely by decree. Frederick’s potato decree simply told farmers what they now had to plant.

Prussia was a powerful kingdom in northern Europe, centred on Berlin, that no longer exists on a map. In 1871 it pulled the German states together into one country, and Germany is what grew out of it. Frederick the Great was its king in the 1700s.

Lore is the collection of stories and beliefs a group of people pass along by telling each other, rather than by writing them down and checking them. Local lore has it that means the locals tell this story, but nobody can prove it. The tale about the king guarding potato fields so farmers would want to steal them may be true or may just be a good story.

To be sweet on something or someone is to be fond of them. It is a slightly old-fashioned, affectionate phrase, most often used about having a crush on a person. Visitors sweet on potatoes are people who love the crop enough to leave one on a king’s grave.

Sanssouci was Frederick the Great’s summer palace in Potsdam, just outside Berlin, and he is buried in its grounds. The name is French for without worries, which was the sort of place he wanted it to be. Visitors still leave potatoes on his grave as a thank-you.
